Can Corning's AT&T Deal Boost Its Optical Communications Growth?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:40 AM PDT 2 min read
Corning Incorporated GLW has secured a multi-year agreement worth more than $3 billion with AT&T Inc. T to expand high-speed broadband infrastructure in the United States. The deal strengthens Corning's position in optical communications as rising data consumption and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption drive greater demand for advanced connectivity.
Under the agreement, Corning will provide the fiber and cable required for AT&T's network expansion, supporting connectivity for residential customers, businesses and communities. Its fiber and connectivity solutions are expected to accelerate network deployment, improve installation efficiency and support the domestic connectivity supply chain.
Corning is also expanding its fiber and cable production in the United States, including a North Carolina facility that has created hundreds of jobs. These investments will increase the company's manufacturing capacity and strengthen its ability to supply fiber solutions for next-generation network infrastructure.
Corning has also partnered with Verizon Communications Inc. VZ to provide fiber and connectivity solutions for broadband expansion and AI-related infrastructure. As telecom companies continue to invest in higher-capacity networks, Corning is likely to benefit from sustained demand for optical fiber and related solutions, supporting its growth opportunities in the communications market.
How Are Competitors Focusing on Fiber?
Corning faces competition from Amphenol Corporation APH and Lumen Technologies, Inc. LUMN. Amphenol is strengthening its fiber-optic capabilities to meet growing demand from data centers and AI applications. The company is seeing strong demand for fiber-based connectivity as customers upgrade networks to support higher data speeds and capacity. Amphenol's expanding portfolio of fiber-optic and interconnect products helps meet the growing need for reliable, high-speed data transmission.
Lumen is adding new fiber routes and network capacity as AI workloads drive greater data traffic across the United States. Its NorthLine project will connect Seattle and Minneapolis through a low-latency route designed to support high-capacity data movement between data centers and cloud networks. Lumen is expanding its network infrastructure to meet the growing connectivity needs of businesses, data centers and AI applications.
Corning's Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Corning have rallied 85.0% over the past year compared with the industry's growth of 130.4%.
From a valuation standpoint, the company's shares currently trade at 38.14 forward 12-month earnings, higher than the industry tally of 35.07.
Corning's earnings estimates for 2026 have increased 0.9% to $3.28 per share, while the same for 2027 have risen 0.7% to $4.28 over the past 60 days.

Coherent's PhotonLink platform and a fresh Wall Street initiation sent optics stocks surging well ahead of the broader market, raising the question of whether this rally signals a durable AI infrastructure trade or another sentiment-driven spike.
Published October 1, 2026, 10:56am ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR | COHR Price Prediction) stock jumped 10% to $315.71 as traders focused on the company’s PhotonLink platform and fresh Wall Street support for AI infrastructure suppliers. Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) stock rose 9% to $1,058.42, while Corning (NYSE:GLW) stock advanced 3% to $158.89.
The broader optics rally outpaced the market. The Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (CBOE:LYTE) gained 4% to $25.40, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) slipped 0.2% to $761.11.
Coherent introduced PhotonLink in September as an integrated-optics platform for next-generation AI data centers. The company also expanded its Pluggable Optical Line System portfolio, linking chip-to-chip, inside-the-rack, and high-capacity data-center connectivity products to the same AI infrastructure buildout.
PhotonLink highlights Coherent’s vertically integrated position across materials, lasers, optics, specialty fibers, and related manufacturing capabilities. Coherent said the platform includes more than 10 customer engagements for co-packaged optics and more than 10 customer engagements for near-packaged optics.
AI data centers require more bandwidth and more efficient connections as workloads become larger and more complex. Coherent could benefit if hyperscalers and equipment makers accelerate deployments of advanced optical components, though the company must turn early engagement into sustained orders and profitable production.
Bernstein initiated coverage of Coherent with an Outperform rating as part of broader coverage of U.S. networking and optical companies. Bernstein said networking and optical suppliers could be “structural winners” within AI infrastructure, an assessment that helped reinforce investor interest in Coherent stock.
The research firm also began coverage of Lumentum, Ciena Corporation (NYSE:CIEN), and Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) with Outperform ratings. Bernstein initiated Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Corning with Market Perform ratings, providing a more balanced view of an industry that has rallied sharply on AI-related expectations.
Coherent stock’s 10% gain exceeded the 4% move in the LYTE ETF, suggesting that PhotonLink and Bernstein’s favorable initiation gave traders a company-specific reason to bid up the shares. Still, Coherent stock can remain sensitive to shifts in AI capital-spending expectations, customer order timing, and concerns about industry capacity.
Lumentum stock climbed 9% to $1,058.42, extending the recovery that began after a recent optics-sector selloff. Lumentum reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $1.006 billion, up 109.3% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share of $3.23 exceeded the $2.97 consensus estimate.
The company guided for fiscal first-quarter revenue between $1.225 billion and $1.275 billion. Lumentum management said demand signals for 2027 remained “incredibly strong,” while the company also reported that optical-circuit-switch shipments doubled from the fiscal third quarter to the fiscal fourth quarter.
Lumentum could benefit from demand for high-speed networking, optical switching, transceivers, and other hardware needed to connect AI computing systems. Yet Lumentum faces execution risk as the company expands output, with management previously acknowledging that shipments of high-powered lasers were behind demand.
Corning stock rose 3%, a smaller gain than Coherent stock and Lumentum stock but still well ahead of the SPY ETF’s 0.2% decline. Corning supplies specialty glass, fiber, and optical communications products, giving Corning multiple ways to participate in higher data-center connectivity spending.
The LYTE ETF’s 4% advance suggests the market’s buying interest extended beyond a single company. Coherent stock, Lumentum stock, and Corning stock all moved higher as traders returned to a group that benefits from expectations for rising AI network traffic and increasingly demanding data-center architectures.
The Coherent stock rally could continue if AI-related orders, customer commentary, and capital-spending plans remain supportive. However, the same theme creates risk if large customers delay infrastructure spending, if competitors build excess capacity, or if elevated expectations leave less room for execution mistakes.
Coherent has a compelling product catalyst in PhotonLink and a new Outperform rating to support the bullish discussion. Investors should watch for signs that the company’s customer engagements become material revenue opportunities, while keeping position sizes modest because optics stocks can move sharply as sentiment toward the AI trade changes.

Corning and AT&T's $3 Billion Fiber Deal Reveals Where AI Spending Goes Next
Corning and AT&T's $3 Billion Fiber Deal Reveals Where AI Spending Goes Next
As AI drives unprecedented data demand, Corning’s $3 billion fiber deal with AT&T highlights the shift from chips to the physical networks that connect them. But soaring growth expectations bring valuation and dilution risks for investors.

Corning and AT&T finalized a multi-year fiber supply deal worth more than $3 billion, reflecting rising demand for optical network infrastructure to support AI and cloud growth.
Corning trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 72 amid heavy insider selling and a planned $2 billion stock offering, raising valuation and dilution concerns despite strong revenue growth.
AT&T is funding a costly network expansion to handle surging data usage, but it offers a lower valuation, a 4.46% dividend yield, and a well-covered payout ratio.
Special Report: Elon Musk’s Hushed FCC Filing. Dec 8th. (From Paradigm Press)
The artificial intelligence (AI) build-out has historically focused on the semiconductor sector, driving valuations to historic premiums as capital chased processing power. However, processing capabilities hold limited utility without the physical infrastructure required to transmit staggering data volumes.
The optical communications supply chain represents the next essential phase of this investment cycle. Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW) and AT&T Inc. (NYSE: T) recently finalized a multi-year fiber supply agreement valued at more than $3 billion. This contract marks a transition from speculative hardware multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation networks. As data consumption surges, securing the physical pathways for cloud and AI integration becomes paramount. Investors evaluating infrastructure plays can look to these developments as a roadmap for where institutional capital is flowing next.
The $100 Stock Behind Elon's Next Move (Ad)
A small, publicly traded supplier trading under $100 a share has reportedly worked alongside Elon Musk for more than a decade.
A federal filing may outline Musk's next major move: an AI network of up to a million satellites powered by the sun. James Altucher says this supplier holds the piece Musk doesn't own.
Watch James Altucher's free Masterclass on this Musk-linked supplier stock
Analyzing the transition from speculative semiconductor multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation optical networks reveals a changing landscape. Corning operates as a primary bottleneck supplier for telecommunications network expansion and hyperscaler data center infrastructure.
AT&T's recent $3 billion commitment follows a similar multi-billion-dollar fiber supply contract with Verizon (NYSE: VZ) and prior commitments, including a $6 billion agreement with Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) for data center optics.
These supply agreements create a multi-year locked backlog, turning uncertain sector demand into highly visible forward revenue. With multiple major technology and telecommunications entities competing for optical fiber, Corning has consolidated the physical supply chain.
The financial impact of this demand is already materializing in Corning's performance. During the second quarter of 2026, Corning reported a 17.1% year-over-year revenue increase, reaching roughly $4.74 billion. Earnings per share came in at 78 cents, beating consensus estimates of 76 cents. Management projects an annualized sales run rate nearing $20 billion by the end of 2026, scaling toward roughly $40 billion by 2030.
The AT&T deal allows Corning to maximize capacity utilization at its newly announced optical manufacturing plants in North Carolina and Texas. Higher utilization rates and fixed-cost absorption directly catalyze EBITDA margin expansion in the optical communications segment. Expanding these margins creates a clearer pathway to sustained profitability as production scales.
The underlying driver for this infrastructure deployment is an escalating network load. The average AT&T fiber household currently consumes over one terabyte of data monthly, marking a roughly 500% increase since 2016.
AT&T's internal projections point to household consumption reaching roughly 2.0 to 2.5 terabytes per month by 2030. Cloud computing, constant video streaming, and the broad integration of enterprise artificial intelligence tools accelerate this baseline usage.
To support this data density, AT&T has mandated a network expansion to reach 60 million passings by 2030. The recent acquisition of Lumen's mass market fiber business for approximately $5.75 billion requires substantial physical hardware integration to meet these targets. AT&T absorbs the upfront capital expenditure required for this expansion and secures the fiber needed from Corning.
During the second quarter of 2026, AT&T generated roughly $31.56 billion in revenue and reported earnings per share of 65 cents, beating consensus estimates of 59 cents. Carrying this infrastructure load impacts the balance sheet. AT&T's net debt currently sits near 2.68 times EBITDA, slightly above its internal target of 2.5 times. Despite the debt load, AT&T trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 8.4, paired with a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of approximately 1.26. AT&T maintains an annual dividend payout of $1.11 per share, yielding approximately 4.46%. The payout ratio stands at roughly 36.7% of earnings, suggesting the dividend remains well-covered even amid heavy capital deployment.

Pricing in the Perfection of a Locked Backlog
While Corning's fundamental business benefits from a guaranteed order book, the market has priced in this optimism. Following a notable rally over the past year, Corning trades at a price-to-earnings ratio hovering around 72. This multiple matches or exceeds many pure-play semiconductor and AI hardware manufacturers.
Forward metrics indicate expected earnings growth near 30.5% year over year, which helps contextualize the premium, but the valuation leaves little room for execution errors. Short interest sits at about 17.6 million shares, or roughly 2.1% of the float, reflecting a recent 12% decline as bears cover positions amid strong contract announcements.
Corporate insiders at Corning have executed selling programs throughout the year, suggesting leadership views the current share price as fully valued. Over the trailing 12-month period, insiders liquidated nearly $80 million in equity. Notable transactions include the chief operating officer selling 100,000 shares in June, and an executive vice president offloading 13,100 shares at an average price near $151.29 in August 2026.
Compounding the valuation concerns, Corning filed an at-the-market equity distribution agreement with Goldman Sachs on Sept. 11, 2026, to sell up to $2 billion in new common stock. This filing introduces immediate dilution risk for existing shareholders. Companies often utilize at-the-market offerings to raise capital when they believe their stock commands a market premium. The cash influx will likely fund the manufacturing scale required for the AT&T and Meta contracts, but it requires current investors to accept a smaller slice of future earnings.
Finding the Margin of Safety in AI Infrastructure
Physical fiber deployment is an inescapable prerequisite for the next generation of digital infrastructure. The resulting capital expenditure boom secures Corning's order book and provides exceptional forward revenue visibility that most hardware manufacturers struggle to achieve.
Telecommunications operators like AT&T must upgrade their networks to prevent service degradation and remain competitive, effectively guaranteeing a steady stream of purchase orders for fiber suppliers. Investors evaluating the artificial intelligence and broad connectivity theme face a clear divergence in risk profiles.
The physical hardware supplier offers a high-growth, high-multiple entry point with established dilution risks and heavy insider selling. Conversely, the telecommunications operator absorbs upfront deployment costs but offers a highly compressed valuation multiple and a steady dividend yield. Investors mapping out infrastructure exposure might consider how these distinct profiles fit within a broader portfolio allocation strategy, balancing the supplier's premium growth against the network operator's value-oriented cash flows.

Reading AI Data Centers through 'Power and Light'—Earnings Analysis of Eaton, Corning, and Fujikura, and the Pitfalls of Growth Stocks
AI Infrastructure & Advanced Stock Lab | Structural Analysis of Earnings and Finance
Information Verification Date: October 2, 2026. Performance comparisons are generally based on the three-month period from April to June 2026 versus the same period in the previous year. Company forecasts and estimates based on our lab's calculations and assumptions are noted separately.
※ This article is for general information purposes intended for corporate analysis. It does not recommend buying or selling specific stocks or suggest timing for such trades. Please also read the notes at the end.

Buying GPUs does not complete a data center
Even if high-performance GPUs are procured, they cannot operate if power receiving equipment is not ready. Even if electricity is available, if computers cannot exchange data at sufficient speeds, their computing power cannot be fully utilized.
Therefore, we should focus on equipment that safely distributes power and optical communications that transport massive amounts of data.
However, if you choose stocks solely because they are 'necessary for AI,' you will skip the most critical questions.
When demand increases, how much profit and cash will remain for the company? And to what extent has the stock price already priced in that growth?
In this report, we examine the US-listed Eaton (ETN, headquartered in Ireland), Corning (GLW), and Japan's Fujikura (5803). We will analyze power equipment and optical wiring companies without grouping them into the same 'AI-related' box.
1. Power issues should be divided into total volume, location, and timing
According to the IEA's 2026 updated outlook, global data center power consumption is expected to increase from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh by 2030. This figure covers all data centers, not just AI-specific facilities. Even in 2030, this is estimated to account for about 3% of total global power consumption.Source: IEA 'Key Questions on Energy and AI'
Looking only at the global ratio, it might feel small. However, data centers are concentrated in specific regions. What is needed is not just the amount of power generated somewhere, but the power receiving capacity available at the construction site on the start-up date.
The mismatch between the speed of power system development and data center construction becomes a regional constraint. The IEA also cites connection queues and the misalignment between investment in power facilities and demand as challenges.Source: IEA, same report
Investors should consider that an increase in power generation does not automatically translate into profit for a specific manufacturer. It is necessary to break down who is responsible for transformation, distribution, protection, and backup power, which equipment is in short supply, and who holds pricing power.
2. Optical communication constraints are not just about 'speed'
In optical communication, in addition to the transmission speed per fiber, the issues are how much wiring can be accommodated in limited conduits and racks, and how quickly and accurately connections can be made on-site.
In its 2026 technology outlook, Corning explains connections between data centers, between switches, and within racks separately. While high density and installation burdens are challenges, they do not view copper wiring within racks as being immediately and entirely replaced by optical fiber.Source: Corning, 2026 Data Center Technology Outlook
From this, what our lab emphasizes is that products that can reduce customer construction costs and start-up time can generate value that exceeds simple material costs.
However, whether that value remains as profit for the manufacturer is a different matter. As substitutes increase, downward pressure on prices will occur, and if major customers source from multiple companies, their bargaining power will also change.
The ideas that 'optical communication will grow' and 'the profit margins of all optical communication companies will rise' should be verified separately.
[Ad 1 | Learning about the semiconductor industry background]
'Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology' by Chris Miller, translated by Toshio Chiba.
This is a related book for those who want to know the history of semiconductor technology and international supply chains. It is not the source of the earnings figures in this article.Publisher's introduction
3. Five indicators to check in earnings reports
Basic interpretation: Are the candidates for future sales increasing?
Common pitfalls: Backlog increases even with longer lead times. Cancellation terms and the impact of acquisitions are also necessary.
Basic interpretation: The percentage of profit remaining after subtracting the cost of goods sold from sales.
Common pitfalls: Do not call the company-wide gross margin the gross margin of the AI business.
Basic interpretation: Which business generates profit?
Common pitfalls: Do not mix up operating profit with after-tax segment profit.
Basic interpretation: Is future supply capacity being secured?
Common pitfalls: Construction expenditure and the start of mass production occur at different times. Startup costs are also incurred.
Basic interpretation: Is profit being collected as cash?
Common pitfalls: Do not treat an increase in cash flow from advance payments as a permanent increase in profit.
Orders received are orders taken during a certain period, and the backlog is the unfulfilled orders remaining at the end of the period. The book-to-bill ratio is the multiplier obtained by dividing orders received by sales; if it is over 1, it indicates that orders exceeded sales for the same period. However, figures with different aggregation periods or target businesses cannot be compared.
Capital expenditure is not always 'the more, the better.' If demand continues as expected, it leads to an increase in supply capacity, but if demand slows down, depreciation and excess capacity will put pressure on profits.
For example, even if sales increase from 100 to 120, if the gross margin drops from 40% to 30%, the gross profit decreases from 40 to 36. These are hypothetical figures, but they clearly show why profitability cannot be judged by the sales growth rate alone.
[Ad 2 | Organizing the difference between profit and cash]
'New Edition: Understanding the Three Financial Statements' by Katsunori Kunisada.
This is a related book for learning how to connect the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement. It is for basic study for those who want to read news about increased orders and profit growth, including the cash flow situation.Publisher's introduction
In the paid section, I will use the earnings reports of these three companies to compare changes in profit margins, the visibility of orders, and the basis for their competitive advantages. Furthermore, I will use company forecasts and stated assumptions to calculate stock price sensitivity in the event that growth expectations are stripped away.
What remains after you finish reading are verification items that can be updated with the next earnings report. I will structure this in a way that can be used both when tracking corporate growth and when considering whether you are overpaying for that growth.

Corning wins over $3bn AT&T fiber deal on data demand
By Martin Holloway29/09/2026No Comments4 Mins Read
Corning (GLW) has landed an AT&T fiber deal worth more than $3bn, the two companies said on 29 September 2026. AT&T will procure fibre and cable from Corning under a multi-year supply agreement, as first reported by Reuters.
Corning shares climbed 4.01% to $157.60 by 16:00 UTC on the day of the announcement, having risen 3.3% in premarket trading, according to Reuters. The move came despite the stock sitting 6.07% below its 20-day range ahead of the news.
An AT&T fiber deal that dwarfs the 2024 tie-up
GLW over the last month, hourly closes. Source: consolidated US exchange data.
Neither company disclosed the contract’s exact duration or annual value. But the new agreement marks a sharp escalation from a prior AT&T-Corning fibre commitment of more than $1bn struck in 2024, according to Converge Digest. Broadband Breakfast reported that terms beyond the headline figure were withheld by both parties, a gap that leaves the near-term revenue cadence for Corning’s optical business unclear.
AT&T pointed to data volumes as the driver. The average AT&T Fibre household now uses more than one terabyte of data a month, five times the level in 2016, Reuters reported, with usage expected to keep rising as AI, cloud and streaming traffic grows.
Fibre build-out fits a wider spending push
The deal sits inside a much larger AT&T infrastructure programme. The carrier has committed more than $250bn over five years to strengthen US connectivity, and it closed a $5.75bn acquisition of Lumen’s fibre business to extend its network footprint, per Reuters. AT&T has said the build-out supports a goal of bringing fast, reliable internet to 60 million Americans by the end of 2030, according to the companies’ joint release carried by PR Newswire.
For Corning, the contract lands as its earnings recover from a volatile patch. Net income swung from a loss of $117m in the third quarter of 2024 to $559m in the second quarter of 2026, according to filings with the SEC. Diluted earnings per share over the same run moved from a 14-cent loss to 64 cents. Against that backdrop, a supply commitment north of $3bn — even spread across several years — represents a meaningful anchor for the optical communications division.
No sign of a pre-announcement short squeeze
Corning Inc /Ny revenue by quarter, as filed. Source: SEC EDGAR.
Trading data show no unusual positioning ahead of the news. Corning’s short-sale ratio, tracked by FINRA, moved between roughly 0.35 and 0.52 in the ten sessions to 28 September, in line with its recent range rather than spiking as the deal took shape. That suggests the share reaction reflected the announcement itself rather than any leak or pre-positioning by short sellers.
The Wall Street Journal separately confirmed the more-than-$3bn valuation in its own report on the tie-up, adding to a run of same-day coverage that left the core numbers uncontested even as duration and per-year terms stayed private.
The open question for investors is cadence: how the $3bn-plus commitment breaks down year by year, and how much of it lands in Corning’s results before 2030. Neither company has set a date for further disclosure, and the next scheduled data point is Corning’s following quarterly filing with the SEC, where any change in backlog or customer concentration tied to AT&T would typically surface first.
Until then, the market has taken the headline number at face value. Corning’s shares closed the announcement session near the top of their recent trading band, with the stock’s 20-day high sitting at $170.00 — a level traders will watch if fresh detail on the AT&T contract emerges.

Investors often weigh the stability of an industrial giant against the growth potential of a specialized materials leader. Choosing between Corning (GLW +2.35%) and Honeywell International (HON +0.09%) requires balancing two very different business models.
Corning provides the literal glass and fiber backbone for modern electronics and data centers. Honeywell serves as a massive industrial conglomerate managing everything from airplane cockpits to smart building systems. Both companies are essential to global infrastructure but offer distinct risk and reward profiles.
Corning designs and manufactures specialized glass and optical-physics products. It operates as a vital link for tech stocks by supplying optical fiber to Verizon and durable cover glass to Apple (AAPL +1.02%). The company also partners with Amazon (AMZN +1.32%), Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), and Qualcomm (QCOM +1.53%) to support artificial intelligence and data center architectures.
Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, particularly in the display and automotive segments. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company reported revenue of nearly $15.6 billion. This represented revenue growth of approximately 19.1% compared to the prior year. Net income reached roughly $1.6 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 10.2% for the period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.9x. This indicates the company holds roughly $0.90 of debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at 1.6x, meaning it has $1.60 in current assets for every dollar of short-term liabilities. Corning generated nearly $1.4 billion in free cash flow, which is the cash remaining after paying for operations and equipment.
Honeywell International operates as a diversified industrial technology company. It manages four primary segments, including aerospace technologies, industrial automation, and building automation. The company maintains a significant strategic agreement with Bombardier (BDRBF -1.15%) for propulsion and avionics systems. Honeywell is also refining its portfolio by divesting its warehouse and workflow solutions business to focus on higher-growth areas.
In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, Honeywell reported revenue of approximately $37.4 billion. This figure reflected revenue growth of nearly 7.8% over the previous fiscal year. The company achieved a net income of roughly $4.7 billion for the year. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 12.6%, which measures the portion of sales remaining after all expenses are paid.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 2.2x. This indicates that the company's debts are more than double the company's shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 1.3x, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations. Honeywell generated close to $5.4 billion in free cash flow, providing significant capital for dividends and acquisitions.
Corning faces risks related to its highly concentrated customer base. A small number of end customers account for more than half of sales in its display and automotive segments. The company also deals with supply chain sensitivities regarding raw materials and energy costs. Geopolitical risks are prominent due to its manufacturing footprint in the Asia Pacific region, which could be impacted by trade policies or tariffs.
Honeywell faces financial exposure from ongoing litigation, such as matters involving Flexjet. The company is currently managing several operational divestitures, which creates execution risk during the portfolio realignment process. Cybersecurity and regulatory compliance also remain critical, especially under rigorous government contracts. Additionally, segments like commercial aviation are subject to cyclicality and fluctuations in broader economic demand.
Honeywell looks cheaper on most metrics, with a lower Forward P/E and a significantly lower P/S ratio.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Corning got its start manufacturing glass for light bulbs, railroad signals, and tableware. Today, its products have a more technology-oriented focus, most notably optical fiber for data transmission. It also makes laboratory products and glass used in electronic device displays. That positions Corning to benefit from the continuing expansion of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data centers, and 5G telecommunications.
But that doesn't make its prospects unbreakable. Corning depends heavily on a relatively small number of large customers, and demand from the technology sector can be cyclical. The company also faces supply chain risks and carries significant debt relative to its shareholders' equity.
Honeywell, meanwhile, produces equipment and software serving four primary markets: aviation, building automation, industrial automation, and energy and sustainability solutions. Its aviation business in particular has provided steady growth and recurring demand. However, aerospace is also cyclical, and Honeywell faces litigation and regulatory risks.
Corning offers greater upside potential from AI infrastructure and the growing demand for optical connectivity, but that opportunity comes with greater risk. Honeywell is far from a perfect investment, but it is the steadier and more defensive choice. Personally, I have considerable confidence in the near-term growth of AI and data-center infrastructure, so Corning is where I would allocate a small, speculative portion of my portfolio.

AT&T signs $3 billion fiber supply deal with Corning

AT&T announced a multi-year supply agreement with Corning Incorporated on Tuesday valued at more than $3 billion, under which Corning will provide the fiber and cable AT&T needs to expand its network as demand for data-intensive services grows.
The deal supports AT&T's goal of reaching 60 million fiber locations by the end of 2030, the company said. AT&T said the typical household on its fiber network now consumes over a terabyte of data monthly, a fivefold increase since 2016, and the company projects that consumption will rise to somewhere between 2 and 2.5 terabytes per month by 2030.
"Fiber remains the gold standard for superior internet connectivity, and AT&T is the nation's leader in fiber," AT&T Chairman and CEO John Stankey said in a statement. "We deeply value our long and successful relationship with Corning and look forward to continuing our work together as we expand the nation's largest fiber network."
Corning Chairman, CEO, and President Wendell Weeks said in a statement that the agreement is "the next chapter" in a partnership spanning generations. "By pairing our large, U.S.-based advanced manufacturing with AT&T's network leadership, we can keep co-innovating to build the dense fiber networks that will drive the future of connectivity," Weeks said.
Both companies framed the deal as a boost to domestic manufacturing and employment. Corning produces the fiber at U.S. facilities, including operations in North Carolina, while AT&T's installation and maintenance workforce is the telecom industry's largest union-represented workforce, the company said. AT&T has committed more than $250 billion over five years to U.S. connectivity infrastructure.
AT&T said the financial impact of the agreement is already reflected in the outlook it provided with its second-quarter 2026 earnings, and the company reiterated that guidance.
The deal extends a run of large supply agreements for Corning. The company struck a multiyear, multibillion-dollar agreement with Amazon to supply optical fiber, cable, and connectivity solutions for Amazon's U.S. data centers, a deal that included plans to create 1,000 jobs at Corning's North Carolina manufacturing facilities. Corning has also announced agreements with Nvidia, valued at as much as $3.2 billion, and an earlier deal with Meta worth up to $6 billion.
Corning's Optical Communications segment posted net sales of $2.07 billion in the second quarter, up 32% from a year earlier, the company said. In reporting those results, Corning projected a sales compound annual growth rate of 19% from the fourth quarter of 2026 through the fourth quarter of 2030, targeting annualized sales of $40 billion by the end of that period.

Can Corning's AT&T Deal Boost Its Optical Communications Growth?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:40 AM PDT 2 min read
Corning Incorporated GLW has secured a multi-year agreement worth more than $3 billion with AT&T Inc. T to expand high-speed broadband infrastructure in the United States. The deal strengthens Corning's position in optical communications as rising data consumption and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption drive greater demand for advanced connectivity.
Under the agreement, Corning will provide the fiber and cable required for AT&T's network expansion, supporting connectivity for residential customers, businesses and communities. Its fiber and connectivity solutions are expected to accelerate network deployment, improve installation efficiency and support the domestic connectivity supply chain.
Corning is also expanding its fiber and cable production in the United States, including a North Carolina facility that has created hundreds of jobs. These investments will increase the company's manufacturing capacity and strengthen its ability to supply fiber solutions for next-generation network infrastructure.
Corning has also partnered with Verizon Communications Inc. VZ to provide fiber and connectivity solutions for broadband expansion and AI-related infrastructure. As telecom companies continue to invest in higher-capacity networks, Corning is likely to benefit from sustained demand for optical fiber and related solutions, supporting its growth opportunities in the communications market.
How Are Competitors Focusing on Fiber?
Corning faces competition from Amphenol Corporation APH and Lumen Technologies, Inc. LUMN. Amphenol is strengthening its fiber-optic capabilities to meet growing demand from data centers and AI applications. The company is seeing strong demand for fiber-based connectivity as customers upgrade networks to support higher data speeds and capacity. Amphenol's expanding portfolio of fiber-optic and interconnect products helps meet the growing need for reliable, high-speed data transmission.
Lumen is adding new fiber routes and network capacity as AI workloads drive greater data traffic across the United States. Its NorthLine project will connect Seattle and Minneapolis through a low-latency route designed to support high-capacity data movement between data centers and cloud networks. Lumen is expanding its network infrastructure to meet the growing connectivity needs of businesses, data centers and AI applications.
Corning's Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Corning have rallied 85.0% over the past year compared with the industry's growth of 130.4%.
From a valuation standpoint, the company's shares currently trade at 38.14 forward 12-month earnings, higher than the industry tally of 35.07.
Corning's earnings estimates for 2026 have increased 0.9% to $3.28 per share, while the same for 2027 have risen 0.7% to $4.28 over the past 60 days.

Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR | COHR Price Prediction) stock jumped 10% to $315.71 as traders focused on the company’s PhotonLink platform and fresh Wall Street support for AI infrastructure suppliers. Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) stock rose 9% to $1,058.42, while Corning (NYSE:GLW) stock advanced 3% to $158.89.
The broader optics rally outpaced the market. The Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (CBOE:LYTE) gained 4% to $25.40, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) slipped 0.2% to $761.11.
Coherent introduced PhotonLink in September as an integrated-optics platform for next-generation AI data centers. The company also expanded its Pluggable Optical Line System portfolio, linking chip-to-chip, inside-the-rack, and high-capacity data-center connectivity products to the same AI infrastructure buildout.
PhotonLink highlights Coherent’s vertically integrated position across materials, lasers, optics, specialty fibers, and related manufacturing capabilities. Coherent said the platform includes more than 10 customer engagements for co-packaged optics and more than 10 customer engagements for near-packaged optics.
AI data centers require more bandwidth and more efficient connections as workloads become larger and more complex. Coherent could benefit if hyperscalers and equipment makers accelerate deployments of advanced optical components, though the company must turn early engagement into sustained orders and profitable production.
Bernstein initiated coverage of Coherent with an Outperform rating as part of broader coverage of U.S. networking and optical companies. Bernstein said networking and optical suppliers could be “structural winners” within AI infrastructure, an assessment that helped reinforce investor interest in Coherent stock.
The research firm also began coverage of Lumentum, Ciena Corporation (NYSE:CIEN), and Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) with Outperform ratings. Bernstein initiated Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Corning with Market Perform ratings, providing a more balanced view of an industry that has rallied sharply on AI-related expectations.
Coherent stock’s 10% gain exceeded the 4% move in the LYTE ETF, suggesting that PhotonLink and Bernstein’s favorable initiation gave traders a company-specific reason to bid up the shares. Still, Coherent stock can remain sensitive to shifts in AI capital-spending expectations, customer order timing, and concerns about industry capacity.
Lumentum stock climbed 9% to $1,058.42, extending the recovery that began after a recent optics-sector selloff. Lumentum reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $1.006 billion, up 109.3% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share of $3.23 exceeded the $2.97 consensus estimate.
The company guided for fiscal first-quarter revenue between $1.225 billion and $1.275 billion. Lumentum management said demand signals for 2027 remained “incredibly strong,” while the company also reported that optical-circuit-switch shipments doubled from the fiscal third quarter to the fiscal fourth quarter.
Lumentum could benefit from demand for high-speed networking, optical switching, transceivers, and other hardware needed to connect AI computing systems. Yet Lumentum faces execution risk as the company expands output, with management previously acknowledging that shipments of high-powered lasers were behind demand.
Corning stock rose 3%, a smaller gain than Coherent stock and Lumentum stock but still well ahead of the SPY ETF’s 0.2% decline. Corning supplies specialty glass, fiber, and optical communications products, giving Corning multiple ways to participate in higher data-center connectivity spending.
The LYTE ETF’s 4% advance suggests the market’s buying interest extended beyond a single company. Coherent stock, Lumentum stock, and Corning stock all moved higher as traders returned to a group that benefits from expectations for rising AI network traffic and increasingly demanding data-center architectures.
The Coherent stock rally could continue if AI-related orders, customer commentary, and capital-spending plans remain supportive. However, the same theme creates risk if large customers delay infrastructure spending, if competitors build excess capacity, or if elevated expectations leave less room for execution mistakes.
Coherent has a compelling product catalyst in PhotonLink and a new Outperform rating to support the bullish discussion. Investors should watch for signs that the company’s customer engagements become material revenue opportunities, while keeping position sizes modest because optics stocks can move sharply as sentiment toward the AI trade changes.

The artificial intelligence (AI) build-out has historically focused on the semiconductor sector, driving valuations to historic premiums as capital chased processing power. However, processing capabilities hold limited utility without the physical infrastructure required to transmit staggering data volumes.
The optical communications supply chain represents the next essential phase of this investment cycle. Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW) and AT&T Inc. (NYSE: T) recently finalized a multi-year fiber supply agreement valued at more than $3 billion. This contract marks a transition from speculative hardware multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation networks. As data consumption surges, securing the physical pathways for cloud and AI integration becomes paramount. Analyzing the transition from speculative semiconductor multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation optical networks reveals a changing landscape. Corning operates as a primary bottleneck supplier for telecommunications network expansion and hyperscaler data center infrastructure.
AT&T's recent $3 billion commitment follows a similar multi-billion-dollar fiber supply contract with Verizon (NYSE: VZ) and prior commitments, including a $6 billion agreement with Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) for data center optics.
These supply agreements create a multi-year locked backlog, turning uncertain sector demand into highly visible forward revenue. With multiple major technology and telecommunications entities competing for optical fiber, Corning has consolidated the physical supply chain.
The financial impact of this demand is already materializing in Corning's performance. During the second quarter of 2026, Corning reported a 17.1% year-over-year revenue increase, reaching roughly $4.74 billion. Earnings per share came in at 78 cents, beating consensus estimates of 76 cents. Management projects an annualized sales run rate nearing $20 billion by the end of 2026, scaling toward roughly $40 billion by 2030.
The AT&T deal allows Corning to maximize capacity utilization at its newly announced optical manufacturing plants in North Carolina and Texas. Higher utilization rates and fixed-cost absorption directly catalyze EBITDA margin expansion in the optical communications segment. Expanding these margins creates a clearer pathway to sustained profitability as production scales.
The underlying driver for this infrastructure deployment is an escalating network load. The average AT&T fiber household currently consumes over one terabyte of data monthly, marking a roughly 500% increase since 2016.
AT&T's internal projections point to household consumption reaching roughly 2.0 to 2.5 terabytes per month by 2030. Cloud computing, constant video streaming, and the broad integration of enterprise artificial intelligence tools accelerate this baseline usage.
To support this data density, AT&T has mandated a network expansion to reach 60 million passings by 2030. The recent acquisition of Lumen's mass market fiber business for approximately $5.75 billion requires substantial physical hardware integration to meet these targets. AT&T absorbs the upfront capital expenditure required for this expansion and secures the fiber needed from Corning.
During the second quarter of 2026, AT&T generated roughly $31.56 billion in revenue and reported earnings per share of 65 cents, beating consensus estimates of 59 cents. Carrying this infrastructure load impacts the balance sheet. AT&T's net debt currently sits near 2.68 times EBITDA, slightly above its internal target of 2.5 times. Despite the debt load, AT&T trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 8.4, paired with a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of approximately 1.26. AT&T maintains an annual dividend payout of $1.11 per share, yielding approximately 4.46%. The payout ratio stands at roughly 36.7% of earnings, suggesting the dividend remains well-covered even amid heavy capital deployment.

Pricing in the Perfection of a Locked Backlog
While Corning's fundamental business benefits from a guaranteed order book, the market has priced in this optimism. Following a notable rally over the past year, Corning trades at a price-to-earnings ratio hovering around 72. This multiple matches or exceeds many pure-play semiconductor and AI hardware manufacturers.
Forward metrics indicate expected earnings growth near 30.5% year over year, which helps contextualize the premium, but the valuation leaves little room for execution errors. Short interest sits at about 17.6 million shares, or roughly 2.1% of the float, reflecting a recent 12% decline as bears cover positions amid strong contract announcements.
Corporate insiders at Corning have executed selling programs throughout the year, suggesting leadership views the current share price as fully valued. Over the trailing 12-month period, insiders liquidated nearly $80 million in equity. Notable transactions include the chief operating officer selling 100,000 shares in June, and an executive vice president offloading 13,100 shares at an average price near $151.29 in August 2026.
Compounding the valuation concerns, Corning filed an at-the-market equity distribution agreement with Goldman Sachs on Sept. 11, 2026, to sell up to $2 billion in new common stock. This filing introduces immediate dilution risk for existing shareholders. Companies often utilize at-the-market offerings to raise capital when they believe their stock commands a market premium. The cash influx will likely fund the manufacturing scale required for the AT&T and Meta contracts, but it requires current investors to accept a smaller slice of future earnings.
Finding the Margin of Safety in AI Infrastructure
Physical fiber deployment is an inescapable prerequisite for the next generation of digital infrastructure. The resulting capital expenditure boom secures Corning's order book and provides exceptional forward revenue visibility that most hardware manufacturers struggle to achieve.
Telecommunications operators like AT&T must upgrade their networks to prevent service degradation and remain competitive, effectively guaranteeing a steady stream of purchase orders for fiber suppliers. Investors evaluating the artificial intelligence and broad connectivity theme face a clear divergence in risk profiles.
The physical hardware supplier offers a high-growth, high-multiple entry point with established dilution risks and heavy insider selling. Conversely, the telecommunications operator absorbs upfront deployment costs but offers a highly compressed valuation multiple and a steady dividend yield. Investors mapping out infrastructure exposure might consider how these distinct profiles fit within a broader portfolio allocation strategy, balancing the supplier's premium growth against the network operator's value-oriented cash flows.

Buying GPUs does not complete a data center
Even if high-performance GPUs are procured, they cannot operate if power receiving equipment is not ready. Even if electricity is available, if computers cannot exchange data at sufficient speeds, their computing power cannot be fully utilized.
Therefore, we should focus on equipment that safely distributes power and optical communications that transport massive amounts of data.

When demand increases, how much profit and cash will remain for the company? And to what extent has the stock price already priced in that growth?
In this report, we examine the US-listed Eaton (ETN, headquartered in Ireland), Corning (GLW), and Japan's Fujikura (5803). We will analyze power equipment and optical wiring companies without grouping them into the same 'AI-related' box.
1. Power issues should be divided into total volume, location, and timing
According to the IEA's 2026 updated outlook, global data center power consumption is expected to increase from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh by 2030. This figure covers all data centers, not just AI-specific facilities. Even in 2030, this is estimated to account for about 3% of total global power consumption.Source: IEA 'Key Questions on Energy and AI'
Looking only at the global ratio, it might feel small. However, data centers are concentrated in specific regions. What is needed is not just the amount of power generated somewhere, but the power receiving capacity available at the construction site on the start-up date.
The mismatch between the speed of power system development and data center construction becomes a regional constraint. The IEA also cites connection queues and the misalignment between investment in power facilities and demand as challenges.Source: IEA, same report
Investors should consider that an increase in power generation does not automatically translate into profit for a specific manufacturer. It is necessary to break down who is responsible for transformation, distribution, protection, and backup power, which equipment is in short supply, and who holds pricing power.
2. Optical communication constraints are not just about 'speed'
In optical communication, in addition to the transmission speed per fiber, the issues are how much wiring can be accommodated in limited conduits and racks, and how quickly and accurately connections can be made on-site.
In its 2026 technology outlook, Corning explains connections between data centers, between switches, and within racks separately. While high density and installation burdens are challenges, they do not view copper wiring within racks as being immediately and entirely replaced by optical fiber.Source: Corning, 2026 Data Center Technology Outlook
From this, what our lab emphasizes is that products that can reduce customer construction costs and start-up time can generate value that exceeds simple material costs.
However, whether that value remains as profit for the manufacturer is a different matter. As substitutes increase, downward pressure on prices will occur, and if major customers source from multiple companies, their bargaining power will also change.
The ideas that 'optical communication will grow' and 'the profit margins of all optical communication companies will rise' should be verified separately.

Corning wins over $3bn AT&T fiber deal on data demand
By Martin Holloway29/09/2026No Comments4 Mins Read
Corning (GLW) has landed an AT&T fiber deal worth more than $3bn, the two companies said on 29 September 2026. AT&T will procure fibre and cable from Corning under a multi-year supply agreement, as first reported by Reuters.
Corning shares climbed 4.01% to $157.60 by 16:00 UTC on the day of the announcement, having risen 3.3% in premarket trading, according to Reuters. The move came despite the stock sitting 6.07% below its 20-day range ahead of the news.
An AT&T fiber deal that dwarfs the 2024 tie-up
GLW over the last month, hourly closes. Source: consolidated US exchange data.
Neither company disclosed the contract’s exact duration or annual value. But the new agreement marks a sharp escalation from a prior AT&T-Corning fibre commitment of more than $1bn struck in 2024, according to Converge Digest. Broadband Breakfast reported that terms beyond the headline figure were withheld by both parties, a gap that leaves the near-term revenue cadence for Corning’s optical business unclear.
AT&T pointed to data volumes as the driver. The average AT&T Fibre household now uses more than one terabyte of data a month, five times the level in 2016, Reuters reported, with usage expected to keep rising as AI, cloud and streaming traffic grows.
Fibre build-out fits a wider spending push
The deal sits inside a much larger AT&T infrastructure programme. The carrier has committed more than $250bn over five years to strengthen US connectivity, and it closed a $5.75bn acquisition of Lumen’s fibre business to extend its network footprint, per Reuters. AT&T has said the build-out supports a goal of bringing fast, reliable internet to 60 million Americans by the end of 2030, according to the companies’ joint release carried by PR Newswire.
For Corning, the contract lands as its earnings recover from a volatile patch. Net income swung from a loss of $117m in the third quarter of 2024 to $559m in the second quarter of 2026, according to filings with the SEC. Diluted earnings per share over the same run moved from a 14-cent loss to 64 cents. Against that backdrop, a supply commitment north of $3bn — even spread across several years — represents a meaningful anchor for the optical communications division.
No sign of a pre-announcement short squeeze
Corning Inc /Ny revenue by quarter, as filed. Source: SEC EDGAR.
Trading data show no unusual positioning ahead of the news. Corning’s short-sale ratio, tracked by FINRA, moved between roughly 0.35 and 0.52 in the ten sessions to 28 September, in line with its recent range rather than spiking as the deal took shape. That suggests the share reaction reflected the announcement itself rather than any leak or pre-positioning by short sellers.
The Wall Street Journal separately confirmed the more-than-$3bn valuation in its own report on the tie-up, adding to a run of same-day coverage that left the core numbers uncontested even as duration and per-year terms stayed private.
The open question for investors is cadence: how the $3bn-plus commitment breaks down year by year, and how much of it lands in Corning’s results before 2030. Neither company has set a date for further disclosure, and the next scheduled data point is Corning’s following quarterly filing with the SEC, where any change in backlog or customer concentration tied to AT&T would typically surface first.
Until then, the market has taken the headline number at face value. Corning’s shares closed the announcement session near the top of their recent trading band, with the stock’s 20-day high sitting at $170.00 — a level traders will watch if fresh detail on the AT&T contract emerges.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Corning got its start manufacturing glass for light bulbs, railroad signals, and tableware. Today, its products have a more technology-oriented focus, most notably optical fiber for data transmission. It also makes laboratory products and glass used in electronic device displays. That positions Corning to benefit from the continuing expansion of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data centers, and 5G telecommunications.
But that doesn't make its prospects unbreakable. Corning depends heavily on a relatively small number of large customers, and demand from the technology sector can be cyclical. The company also faces supply chain risks and carries significant debt relative to its shareholders' equity.
Honeywell, meanwhile, produces equipment and software serving four primary markets: aviation, building automation, industrial automation, and energy and sustainability solutions. Its aviation business in particular has provided steady growth and recurring demand. However, aerospace is also cyclical, and Honeywell faces litigation and regulatory risks.
Corning offers greater upside potential from AI infrastructure and the growing demand for optical connectivity, but that opportunity comes with greater risk. Honeywell is far from a perfect investment, but it is the steadier and more defensive choice. Personally, I have considerable confidence in the near-term growth of AI and data-center infrastructure, so Corning is where I would allocate a small, speculative portion of my portfolio.

bull_case: Corning's $3 billion multi-year fiber supply deal with AT&T provides a clear, large-scale revenue anchor for its optical communications business, directly tied to AI and cloud infrastructure growth. AT&T's fiber household data consumption is projected to reach 2.0-2.5 terabytes monthly by 2030, ensuring sustained demand for Corning's fiber and cable products. The deal also supports Corning's expansion of fiber and cable production in the United States, including a North Carolina facility that created hundreds of jobs, enhancing operational capacity and supply chain resilience.
bear_case: Corning's stock trades at a P/E ratio near 72, matching or exceeding many pure-play semiconductor and AI hardware manufacturers, indicating a premium valuation that leaves little room for execution mistakes. The company is facing a planned $2 billion stock offering, which could dilute existing shareholders and pressure earnings per share. Additionally, AT&T's network expansion requires substantial hardware integration, impacting its balance sheet and potentially leading to slower-than-expected revenue recognition for Corning.
